messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David Mercer, a 63-year-old physician, came to treatment more than a year after surviving a terrorist bombing on a city bus. He had been riding to the hospital for an early shift when two men began shouting at passengers in the aisle. One barked orders for everyone to keep their heads down and stay still, and the sharp authority in that voice had cut through the usual morning noise with a terrifying finality. David remembered the sudden eruption of violence, the crush of bodies trying not to move, the blast itself, and the stunned seconds afterward when the bus seemed to fill with smoke, screams, and commands. He had spent his career moving toward emergencies, but on that morning he was a passenger, trapped and waiting for someone else to decide whether he lived. What stayed with him most was not only the attack but the feeling that ordinary public life had proved fatally deceptive: a routine bus ride, anonymous fellow passengers, a normal workday, and then devastation.

In the weeks afterward, the things that pulled him back into that morning were painfully specific. Riding past a bus stop on his commute made his chest tighten. If a supervisor at the hospital gave brisk instructions in a crowded hallway, he felt himself bracing before he even understood why. News footage of assaults or even raised voices in the emergency department could bring back the same sense that violence could erupt without warning. Those moments did more than upset him; they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe since the attack, that the world was dangerous and that people were not what they seemed. Each trigger landed not as an isolated reminder but as proof, in his mind, that the bombing had revealed the truth about life and had destroyed the safety he once assumed he and his wife lived in.

That way of understanding the trauma hardened over time. David began saying, with flat certainty, that his life had been destroyed by what happened on the bus. He did not mean only that he had suffered; he meant that the basic structure of the world had changed permanently. Because he was convinced danger could be hidden inside ordinary interactions, he found himself scrutinizing strangers’ faces in waiting rooms and elevators, wondering who might be concealing violent intent. A curt instruction from an administrator no longer sounded merely efficient; in an instant it could feel menacing, too close to the shouted commands on the bus. His own beliefs made the triggers easier to find and harder to dismiss. The more certain he became that the world was fundamentally unsafe and other people could not be trusted, the more quickly buses, orders, and any sign of violence stood out to him as charged and intolerable.

At home, those beliefs fed a constant readiness that exhausted both him and his wife. David listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering the house, especially at night, and he remained on guard even in his own living room, as if the boundary between public threat and private safety had been erased. He checked locks repeatedly and reacted sharply to small noises in the driveway. He had come to believe there was no truly secure place anymore, and that conviction kept his body keyed up. His wife noticed how quickly he snapped if she approached him unexpectedly or asked him to lower his voice; his irritability had become one of the most visible ways the trauma now lived in their marriage.

That state of vigilance also fed back into the bleak conclusions he had reached. When he caught himself listening for intruders in his own home, it seemed to him like further evidence that the world really was dangerous. When he felt angry and on edge around people he used to trust, he took that as confirmation that the trauma had ruined his life beyond repair. Even his success at work no longer reassured him. As a doctor, he had started avoiding the bus entirely and driving an indirect route to the hospital, leaving extra early to bypass downtown stops. In the hospital, if voices rose or someone issued forceful instructions during a crisis, he could feel his temper surge and his mind narrow, and afterward he would think, almost bitterly, that this was exactly what the bombing had done to him.

By the time he sought help, his world had become smaller and more suspicious. He was still working, still functioning outwardly, but he was increasingly convinced that danger was everywhere and that no one could be taken at face value. What finally brought him in was his wife telling him that their home no longer felt calm because he never seemed to stand down from alert. David said he was afraid that this was the rest of his life: scanning, bracing, mistrusting, and flaring in anger at the people closest to him. At the same time, he came with a quiet hope that he might not always have to hear an order, see a bus, or catch sight of violence and feel as if he were back in that aisle waiting for the next command.
